sections.title: 7.1 Generalization and optimization theory beyond expressivity
sections.content: Open question. Is there joint, non-vacuous, structure-aware theory that predicts performance and, in slot terms, says which fillers buy task-useful expressivity without paying the complexity penalty? The WeisfeilerLeman and counting ladder in Section 5.5 characterizes what message passing and higher-order extensions can distinguish, but not how trained GNNs generalize. Morris et al. (2024) therefore call for theory combining expressivity, generalization, and the optimization dynamics of stochastic first-order training. Existing VC-dimension, Rademacher-complexity, PAC-Bayes, and covering-number bounds are often vacuous and do not identify the structural statistics governing out-of-sample error (Vasileiou et al., 2025). Carrasco et al. (2025) show that the number of WL-coloring equivalence classes upper-bounds Rademacher complexity. Thus, enriching Pk, Ψk, , or ϕℓ to gain expressivity inflates the complexity term in these worst-case bounds. For sparse, unbounded-size graphs, Amran et al. (2026) establish equicontinuity of message maps under the graphop metric, extending prior limit-based guarantees beyond dense or bounded-size graphs. Whether these bounds are tight enough to guide slot selection remains open. This worst-case inflation is not fundamental. Rauchwerger et al. (2025) construct hierarchical-optimaltransport pseudometric under which message passers are Lipschitz, 1-WL-separating, and defined on relatively compact space, yielding both StoneWeierstrass universal-approximation result and distributionfree generalization bounds. However, this result covers one metric and does not determine which arbitrary slot fillings admit coexistence rather than an inflating Rademacher bound. It is also unknown whether the guarantee survives replacing dense Pk with cheaper operator, linking the problem to Section 7.5.

sections.title: 7.2 Distribution shift and size generalization
sections.content: Open question. Which structural statistics measurably control transfer across graphs of different size or local structure? Distribution shift sharpens this gap. Yehudai et al. (2021) formalize size generalization through local d-patterns and prove that zero-training-loss solutions can fail on larger graphs, with gradient descent empirically converging to them. The failure therefore reflects shift in local structure rather than capacity limit. On biological graphs, Li et al. (2025b) attribute degradation at 210 larger sizes to spectral differences induced by subgraph patterns such as average cycle length, although this account has not been established beyond that domain. Global homophily is likewise unreliable because local homophily varies within graph (Loveland et al., 2024). Recovering an environment-invariant causal subgraph (Chen et al., 2022c) relies on structural-causal-model assumptions challenged by Xu et al. (2024), while method rankings reverse between covariate and concept shift (Gui et al., 2022). The slot-level problem is therefore to identify which Pk and receptive-field domain remain invariant across relevant shift types, including size-induced spectral change.

sections.title: 7.3 Dataset-adaptive slot selection and the fragility of homophily
sections.content: Open question. How can the distribution of task-relevant information across dataset be characterized statistically? No principled map connects measured graph properties to slot choices, and homophily is too fragile to provide one. You et al. (2020) search 315K-design space and transfer designs using task similarity, but the designtask relation remains empirical. Standard homophily measures depend on class count and balance and are not comparable across datasets (Platonov et al., 2023a; Mironov & Prokhorenkova, 2025). Adjusted homophily restores comparability, while label informativeness tracks GNN performance more closely. Under proper tuning, traditional homophily metrics remain unreliable for model selection (Luan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024a). data-centric account instead attributes degradation to under-informative receptive fields rather than smoothing itself (Kormann et al., 2026). Their information distribution is precisely what selection map for Pk, Ψk, and must characterize.

sections.title: 7.4 Automated and causal architecture generation over the slot search space
sections.content: Open question. Can the unified equation, as structured search space, be searched reproducibly, in way that generalizes under shift and is conditioned on data properties rather than spurious correlations? The unified equation defines structured search space. Automated graph learning still lacks tractable graph-specific spaces, scalable search, and principled map from data properties to architectures (Wang et al., 2022b). Without shared space, graph neural architecture search (graph-NAS) results are not comparable, and preferred architectures are dataset-specific (Qin et al., 2022). Graph-NAS can also learn non-causal, distribution-specific grapharchitecture correlations that fail under shift. Causal-subgraph conditioning addresses this failure but leaves environment-free selection open (Li et al., 2025c). Language-model controllers can adapt search from problem and space descriptions, but provide no correctness or optimality guarantees and remain limited by coverage and search cost (Gao et al., 2025). What is missing is causal, data-conditioned, and language-steerable search procedure over the full tuple (X , K, {Pk}, {Ψk}, , Bℓ, ϕℓ) that generalizes under shift.

sections.title: 7.5 Scaling the propagation operator and the cost of global attention
sections.content: Open question. Is dense, quadratic all-pairs attention necessary to capture global context, or can structured sub-quadratic operator match it within an O(n) budget? Scaling fixed architecture raises an expressivityefficiency problem primarily at Pk. Polynomial linear attention and global convolution reduce cost, with the latter reporting 169 speedup over optimized dense attention on two-million-node synthetic graph, but neither characterizes the expressivity sacrificed by linearity (Deng et al., 2024; Sancak et al., 2025). Million-node training also requires modelsystem co-design, so asymptotic complexity understates practical cost (Zhang et al., 2024). No universal sparsifier exists, and distance-preserving sparsifiers can harm downstream GNNs (Chen et al., 2023d). Graph condensation compresses but can require model-dependent full-graph training (Gupta et al., 2026), and no scalable method dominates the accuracyefficiency frontier (Duan et al., 2022). Offline propagation improves throughput but cannot adapt to inference-time input (Liao et al., 2025). Moreover, fair message-passing tuning largely closes the Long Range Graph Benchmark gap, leaving the need for global Pk unestablished (Tönshoff et al., 2024). The open problem is whether dense all-pairs coupling is necessary and, if so, which sub-quadratic operator preserves its useful expressivity. Compression of is secondary axis.

sections.title: 7.6 Temporal graphs and the carry slot as a memory operator
sections.content: Open question. What is the temporal analogue of the static expressivity ladder, what is the right continuous-time form for B(t), and which temporal ingredients earn their cost? The static carry slot Bℓ in Eq. (3) seeds an update from H(ℓ) and H(0). Dynamic graphs require timeindexed memory operator B(t) that retains and selectively forgets information across irregular events. The temporal problem is therefore an under-specified slot rather than missing one. Walk-aggregating and memory-based temporal GNNs are mutually incomparable, and neither computes girth under temporal WL analogue (Souza et al., 2022). Standard temporal messages also lose event source and target identity, preventing persistent forecasting and moving-average representation. Restoring that identity recovers the capability in one architecture but is not standard across temporal-GNN families (Tjandra et al., 2024). Strong temporal link prediction may require neither recurrent memory nor self-attention, leaving component-level attribution unresolved (Cong et al., 2023). Selective continuous-time state-space memory keyed by inter-event gaps provides one candidate (Li et al., 2025a). However, spatial-temporal distribution shift also requires B(t) to specify which temporal structure remains invariant (Tieu et al., 2025). The seven-component tuple remains intact over time, with Pk(t) carrying time-varying support, Ψk preserving event identity, and Bℓ generalizing to B(t).

sections.title: 7.7 Graph-level readout as the missing pooling slot
sections.content: Open question. Does learned pooling operator help at all? The seven-component equation updates node states but does not include the permutation-invariant readout ρ that maps the final node-state multiset to graph vector. Its hierarchical counterpart Qℓ coarsens the graph between layers (Section 3). Both discard node-level structure, so pooling benchmarks test Qℓ while the same expressivity concern applies to ρ. Replacing learned local pooling with random assignments or complement-graph clustering barely changes standard graph-classification accuracy (Mesquita et al., 2020). Across 17 pooling methods and 28 datasets, no method consistently dominates and unpooled baselines match most of them (Wang et al., 2024c). Featuretopology mismatch explains these marginal or inconsistent gains (von Pichowski et al., 2026). readout can discard expressivity gained through Ψk and ϕℓ. Bianchi & Lachi (2023) provide sufficient preservation conditions, but not an operator that also outperforms global summation. Differentiable soft clustering (Ying et al., 2018b) and the injective sum readout that reaches 1-WL with injective aggregation (Xu et al., 2019b) bracket the design space. Closing this gap needs an expressivity-preserving readout that beats tuned global-sum baseline on leakage-free data. Because ρ lies downstream of the seven layer components, Section 6 correctly marks graph classification as out-of-slot.

sections.title: 7.8 The missing transferable vocabulary for graph foundation models
sections.content: Open question. Which slot fillings should be shared versus adapted across domains? versatile graph foundation model requires shared primitives that transfer across featureand structureheterogeneous graphs, together with positive transfer and predictable data scaling (Mao et al., 2024). Open challenges include structural alignment, semantic heterogeneity, scalable pre-training, and trustworthy evaluation (Liu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025d). unified text-attributed feature and label space currently covers only classification on text-rich graphs (Liu et al., 2024b). Cross-domain pre-training can cause negative transfer, and compatibility cannot yet be predicted priori (Zhao et al., 2024). Structural augmentation provides initial evidence of cross-domain data scaling but not predictive scaling model (Tang et al., 2025). Graphlanguage alignment may also exploit shortcuts rather than genuine structural transfer (Tang et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024b), paralleling Section 7.11.3. The required vocabulary spans H(0), , Pk, and Ψk.

sections.title: 7.9 Trustworthy GNNs and entanglement through the propagation slot
sections.content: Open question. Why does trustworthy graph learning resist any per-axis fix? Message passing propagates sensitive attributes, adversarial perturbations, and structural bias through the same operator. Privacy, robustness, fairness, uncertainty, and accuracy therefore interact rather than forming independent axes (Dai et al., 2024). single adversarial edge can affect an entire receptive field, while neighboring attributes leak and heterophily may amplify or mask the effect (Zhu et al., 2022). Gray-box message-interception certificates exploiting Pk are tighter than conservative black-box certificates (Scholten et al., 2022), yet randomized smoothing can require enough noise to collapse clean accuracy (Lai et al., 2026). Propagation also amplifies sensitive-attribute correlations (Dong et al., 2023), and recursive aggregation retains deleted information through neighbors, obstructing unlearning (Fan et al., 2025). Deep ensembles provide little benefit because independently trained GNNs can undergo epistemic collapse (Vieira et al., 2026). The resulting targets are architecture-aware certification, topology-aware debiasing, verifiable forgetting, and graph-native uncertainty quantification.

sections.title: 7.10 Equivariance level and symmetry relaxation
sections.content: Open question. Which symmetry constraint should Pk and Ψk satisfy, and when should it be relaxed? Geometric GNNs span spectrum of symmetry constraints, leaving an expressivityscalabilitysymmetry trade-off (Duval et al., 2023). Because an equivariant function cannot break an inputs symmetry, exact equivariance cannot select among symmetry-equivalent outcomes (Kaba & Ravanbakhsh, 2023). Learnable relaxation for E(3) GNNs provides one candidate filler (Hofgard et al., 2024). At matched capacity in convolutional image networks, equivariance helps only when aligned with task geometry, and reference-frame symmetry breaking can improve performance (Vadgama et al., 2025). This finding has not been tested directly for graphs. Graph generation. Permutation-invariant diffusion models are harder to train than non-invariant models whose target distributions have fewer modes, although post-hoc permutation can recover invariance (Yan et al., 2024). Evaluation metrics are themselves unstable and can reverse model rankings (OBray et al., 2022). What remains is valid-by-construction, scalable generator and stable metric. At the slot level, task geometry must determine symmetry constraints on Pk and Ψk that guarantee equivariance without preventing the distinction of symmetry-inequivalent configurations.

sections.title: 7.11 Broader Outlook Beyond the Base-Layer Equation
sections.content: The following questions concern systems surrounding graph layer. We use the component vocabulary to locate their graph-side design choices, but the seven-component equation does not represent the complete decoder, retrieval pipeline, or multi-agent controller.

sections.title: 7.11.1 Subgraph selection and propagation for retrieval-grounded generation
sections.content: Open question. Which subgraph should be retrieved, and how should its propagation condition the decoder, when neither the retrieval target nor the coupling has theory yet? Graph retrieval-augmented generation inserts graph operator between corpus and frozen language model to ground generation in explicit structure (Han et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025). Community-structured indexing improves corpus-global queries but fixes graph granularity (Edge et al., 2024). Question-specific subgraph retrieval with propagated embeddings (He et al., 2024b) and GNN reasoning over dense subgraphs with verbalized paths (Mavromatis & Karypis, 2025) likewise choose the retrieved domain heuristically. Agentic methods instead let an LLM beam-search knowledge-graph relations (Sun et al., 2024b) or select tools while updating memory (Jiang et al., 2025). However, prompting or supervised imitation still fixes the exploration policy rather than learning an operator jointly with the decoder. Faithful, interpretable 52 knowledge-graph grounding remains the target (Luo et al., 2024a; Pan et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2024e). The unresolved slot-level problem is joint query-conditioned selection of and Pk to minimize hallucination for fixed decoder.

sections.title: 7.11.2 Personalization by conditioning the operator on the individual
sections.content: Open question. How can per-user conditioning be done under extreme sparsity and drift without retraining the operator per user? Personalization conditions propagation on user profiles and interactions, commonly represented by useritem graph (Wang et al., 2023c). Web-scale graph convolution (Ying et al., 2018a) and minimal neighborhood aggregation for collaborative filtering (He et al., 2020) still learn one shared operator and derive personalization from static user embeddings. This design struggles with cold starts, preference drift, and mismatch between fixed operator and non-stationary (Wu et al., 2023c). Language-model personalization further requires fusing user representations with decoder so that generation, not only ranking, is personalized (Zhang et al., 2025c). Collaborative-filtering retrieval can condition generation on users history and those of similar users, but the fusion remains retrieval-mediated rather than co-designed with the decoder (Shi et al., 2025). The open task is user-conditioned Pk and Ψk over that survive sparsity and drift while supporting personalized generation.

sections.title: 7.11.3 Graphs as a reasoning substrate for language models
sections.content: Open question. What theory would determine which structure given task actually needs? graph over language models intermediate states can structure multi-step reasoning, but its topology is usually hand-designed. Graph-of-thought methods generalize chain and tree prompting through aggregation and refinement, yet user-specified topology prevents attributing gains to measured task properties (Besta et al., 2024). Performance also degrades with graph-problem size (Wang et al., 2023a), and genuine reasoning remains hard to distinguish from shortcut exploitation (Wang et al., 2026b). This calls for task-inferred domain and propagation topology Pk, with intermediate states mixed by into eH and measurable structurequality links.

sections.title: 7.11.4 Language agents as optimizable graphs
sections.content: Open question. What principled map takes task to communication graph, together with credit assignment over it? In graph-structured agent systems, nodes are operations and edges are message channels. Jointly optimizing prompts and edges remains empirical and does not explain which topology task requires or why an edge helps (Zhuge et al., 2024). variational graph auto-encoder can instead generate task-adaptive communication topology (Zhang et al., 2025a). reported collaborative scaling law finds logistic performance growth with agent count and an advantage for irregular, small-world topologies over regular ones (Qian et al., 2025). Yet propagation carries language rather than vectors, leaving no expressivity ladder or account of when denser routing earns its cost. The open target is task-conditioned Pk and Ψk over the operation domain with assignable credit.

sections.title: 7.11.5 Editing and generating networks by treating the model as a graph
sections.content: Open question. What permutation-correct operator can edit, merge, or generate weights while scaling to large models? Representing neurons as nodes and weights as edges lets GNN read and write another models parameters. Existing operators respect neuron-permutation symmetry and process diverse architectures (Kofinas et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2024), but are demonstrated only on small networks. This applies Section 7.10 to 53 weight-space domain and leaves unresolved whether symmetry supplies useful structure at scale or merely constrains capacity. Progress here needs Pk and Ψk over weights that support symmetry-correct parameter editing and generation at language-model scale.

sections.title: 7.12 The evaluation crisis and whether progress can be measured
sections.content: Open question. Can reported gains be reliably attributed to specific slot filling, rather than to tuning effort, benchmark leakage, or metric artifacts? Section 6 shows that protocol validity, fair model comparison, and component attribution are separate requirements. The open problem is to turn that hierarchy into an evaluation design that isolates one filling while preserving realistic data and equal tuning effort. Existing benchmarks also overrepresent small molecules and marginal accuracy, which limits application-grounded and foundation-model evaluation (BechlerSpeicher et al., 2025). Structure-agnostic baselines match or exceed GNNs on several graph-classification benchmarks (Errica et al., 2020), while self-explainable GNNs lack formal faithfulness guarantees (Azzolin et al., 2025). Standard fidelity and sparsity metrics do not test recovery of causal variables, motivating an out-of-distribution-generalization score as causal-validity proxy (Zhang et al., 2026a). Progress therefore requires leakage-free, shift-aware, application-grounded comparisons that vary one component or specified interaction while controlling the remaining architecture and evaluation pipeline. The concern also reaches the taxonomy. Spectral propagation may not be theoretically distinct from spatial message passing for node classification (Jiang et al., 2026). If this critique holds broadly, Family 3 (Spectral) collapses into Family 1 (Spatial) for that setting, requiring task-conditional taxonomy or distinction beyond eigenspace representability.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Graph neural network architectures have multiplied faster than the language used to compare them. We unify covered graph neural layers through seven components consisting of an update domain, channel set, propagation bank, per-channel message maps, channel-mixing operator, ego/residual map, and update map. Function-valued fillings allow the same equation to express local message passing, attention, spectral filtering, global communication, relation-specific channels, higher-order domains, and geometric messages. The mixing operator is component, while eH denotes only its output. Worked reductions of four canonical layers and representative fillings across all seven families make this coverage checkable. The equation defines unified component system. Equivalent factorizations remain possible, while the slot discipline provides consistent assignments for component-level analysis. Under this discipline, differing components identify where the framework records architectural differences. Functional equivalence additionally requires agreement among the internal mechanisms and component interactions that determine the resulting inductive bias. The seven primary-axis families are therefore nonexclusive and remain distinct from reusable operations and problem settings. The unified system supports analysis as well as comparison. Under endpoint-local messages and nodelocal updates, operator support bounds one-layer dependencies and yields necessary full-row condition for one-layer global mixing. In the linear additive regime, raw channel count is non-identifiable, whereas minimum Kronecker channel rank is invariant. These attribution and identifiability results depend on explicitly separating the propagation bank, messages, channels, mixing, and update. More broadly, spectral and topological properties of Pk connect propagation to oversmoothing, oversquashing, heterophilic failure, and expressivity limits. The same vocabulary identifies which component remedy changes, translates documented benchmark evidence descriptively into component choices, and exposes structured combinations for architecture generation. These generated architectures provide formally specified candidates for empirical evaluation. The contribution establishes representation and component-level analysis, while selecting the best filling for dataset remains an empirical inverse problem. Establishing validated map from measurable graph and task properties to component choices requires controlled evidence and robust descriptors, particularly because common statistics such as homophily are fragile. Wherever it appears in cell, eH denotes only the output of and is not an additional component or column. 90 Appendix Operations: Composable Modules The seven families of Appendix are distinguished by which slot of the unified equation (3) carries their defining mechanism; most touch several slots, but one is the locus of what makes the family distinct. The modules in this section are different in kind. Each is reusable edit with primary component or externallocation assignment, applicable across families rather than defining one. modules primary location is where it chiefly acts, not guarantee that it touches nothing else. This is the operative content of the architecture/operation distinction drawn in Section 1.2. family answers what does layer compute?; an operation answers what is bolted onto layer, regardless of which family it belongs to? } (with the scalar coefficients γ(ℓ) We make the distinction precise using the slot vocabulary of Section 3. These seven components comprise the update domain , the channel set K, the operator bank {P(ℓ) folded in), the message map Ψ(ℓ) , the mixing , the ego/residual map Bℓ, and the update ϕℓ. The initial state H(0), optional between-layer coarsening map Qℓ, and post-stack readout ρ are related locations but are not additional members of the seven-component per-layer tuple. Each operation below names its primary component or external location using the vocabulary and placement rules of Section 3. As bookkeeping rule, operations with different primary component assignments suggest compatibility, while two that edit the same component (e.g. two residual schemes both writing Bℓ) must be reconciled by an explicit combination rule in that component. The qualifier is that the components are not fully independent. An operation nominally aimed at one component can reach another (a pairwise positional encoding can enter the attention operator Pk, and state-dependent normalization changes the operator it feeds), so the map is heuristic predicting which add-ons are prima facie compatible, not theorem that different-component edits never interact. Table 11 summarizes the mapping. B.1 Positional and Structural Encodings Message passing on an unattributed graph is blind to position. In an L-layer MPNN, two nodes with isomorphic rooted attributed L-hop neighborhoods receive identical representations, which is the combinatorial root of the expressiveness ceiling discussed in Section 5.5. Positional encodings (PE) and structural encodings (SE) can break this symmetry by injecting per-node feature that depends on where the node sits in the graph (PE) or on the local subgraph around it (SE); whether given encoding actually separates two such nodes depends on the descriptor. Primary location. The message map Ψk, often through the external initial state H(0) that feeds it. Following the fold-in convention of Section 3, an encoding is not new slot. node-level encoding contributes feature matrix Epos Rnp that enters the layer either by concatenation into the initial state, H(0) [X Epos], or by addition into the message map Ψk; its primary component is Ψk, with H(0) recorded as the external input location when the encoding is applied before the stack. It leaves fixed structural operator untouched, since the graph over which messages flow is unchanged and only the node descriptors are augmented. It can, however, change state-dependent operator Pk = Pk(H) indirectly. Enriching the input feeds new descriptors into the attention score, so the encoding reaches Pk through the state even though it is introduced at the input. pairwise encoding edits the operator more directly. relative-distance or edge-structural bias that modulates the attention score enters the operator Pk itself (Graphormers spatial and edge biases (Ying et al., 2021), Table 17), and pairwise feature added on the value side enters the pairwise message Ψk. Only node-level encoding paired with fixed structural operator is operator-preserving; with state-dependent Pk(H) even node-level encoding reaches the operator indirectly, as above. Representative forms. Laplacian eigenvectors give spectral PE. The lowest nontrivial eigenvectors of Lsym (Section 2.7) furnish coordinates that are smooth on the graph. These exclude the nullspace of Lsym, which for graph with components is c-dimensional and spanned by the degree-weighted component indicators D1/21C, reducing to the single vector D1/21 in the connected case. The eigenvectors carry two distinct ambiguities with distinct remedies. simple eigenvector has sign ambiguity, usually mitigated by random sign flipping as training augmentation, and resolved structurally by sign-invariant map. 91 repeated eigenvalue additionally has basis ambiguity. Any orthogonal rotation within its eigenspace is valid, which sign flipping cannot address, and it requires basis-invariant or equivariant map over the whole eigenspace. Random-walk SE (Dwivedi et al., 2022a) uses the diagonal return probabilities [(D1A)k]ii for = 1, . . . , K, encoding the probability-weighted return over closed walks at node (a weighted sum, not an unweighted count). These closed walks include backtracking walks, not only simple cycles. The walk operator matters here. For simple graph (no self-loops in A), the bare D1A (defined on positive degrees, with an explicit convention for isolated nodes) has zero diagonal, so it assigns no probability to staying in place after single step, whereas the augmented D1(A + I) has positive one-step self-transition probability 1/(1 + di) at every node. (At 2 both operators can assign positive return probability via walk out and back; the distinction is specifically about the one-step diagonal.) Distance encodings record shortest-path or resistance distances to set of anchor nodes, which requires an equivariant anchor-selection rule, since arbitrarily indexed anchors would break permutation equivariance. Learned and graph-adaptive variants replace fixed eigenvectors with trainable encodings (Dwivedi et al., 2022a; Kreuzer et al., 2021; Ito et al., 2025; Kanatsoulis et al., 2025). Why it is an operation, not family. PE/SE module composes with GCN, with graph Transformer, or with an equivariant network alike; in its input-augmentation form it changes the values supplied to the components rather than introducing new component. Graph Transformers are prominent consumers because their dense attention has no built-in locality to recover position from, but the module itself is family-agnostic. Link to generated architectures. Because PE/SE modules primary edit is filler for Ψk, or for the external H(0) that feeds it, adopting one reads directly onto the three generation levels of Section 4. Concatenating cataloged encoding, such as Laplacian PE, into family that does not natively carry one recombines an existing filler across families and is level 1 move. Supplying learned or graph-adaptive encoding not yet in the inventory (Ito et al., 2025; Kanatsoulis et al., 2025) as the Ψk filler is instead level 2, provided the resulting layer does not reduce to an existing method. pairwise encoding that reaches Pk rather than Ψk is classified the same way, just against the operator slot. B.2 Graph Rewiring and Virtual Nodes The motivation is oversquashing (Section 5.2). When many long-range signals must pass through structural bottleneck, message passing on the original edges compresses them into fixed-width vector and loses information. Rewiring addresses this by changing the communication operator, which nodes communicate and with what weight, adding, removing, or reweighting edges to ease the bottleneck. It does not necessarily relieve the bottleneck, though, and can trade against faithfulness to the input graph. This is not purely support change. Edge reweighting and the degree renormalization that follows adding or dropping edges also change the operators entries, not only its sparsity pattern. Primary location. The operator bank {P(ℓ) }, by changing the support and/or the scalar weights it is built on (and, when the rewiring adds nodes, the domain ), is exactly the fold-in Section 3 specifies for rewiring. rewiring is static when the support is modified once as preprocessing (the operator bank is rebuilt on the rewired graph and then fixed) and dynamic when the support is modified per layer. Representative forms. Curvature-based methods add edges at negatively curved bottlenecks and optionally drop edges in dense regions (Topping et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023). Spectral methods rewire to increase the spectral gap. The relevant quantity is the lazy or absolute spectral gap that governs mixing time and the expansion-related bounds constraining oversquashing (the ordinary λ2-gap alone is insufficient when negative eigenvalues dominate the spectral radius) (Karhadkar et al., 2023). The gap is not sole determinant, though, since larger gap also accelerates smoothing, so the two pathologies trade off rather than improving together. Delay-based and dynamic schemes let the effective support grow with depth so that distant nodes connect only in later layers (Gutteridge et al., 2023). virtual node is the limiting case. It is single node connected to all others, which in the terms of Section 3 enlarges the domain and gives every pair two-hop path i. This is distinct from adding dense global channel directly in Pk, which couples all pairs in one hop. The virtual node instead routes through an extra vertex, so hj reaches only after two synchronous layers (unless the virtual state was already aggregated), as the one-layer mixing analysis of Appendix notes. It is also the cleanest bridge to graph Transformers. The virtual node opens global communication channel that can simulate global interaction under suitable depth, width, and update capacity, though single token is not in general equivalent to arbitrary pairwise attention (Cai et al., 2023). Caution. Rewiring trades faithfulness to the input graph for information flow. When the task actually depends on the original topology, rewiring can hurt; the operation is justified by diagnosed bottleneck, not applied by default. Edge-dropping variants carry further, more basic risk. Removing edges in dense regions without connectivity safeguard can disconnect component or isolate node, which the addition side of curvatureand spectral-based rewiring does not by itself prevent. Link to generated architectures. Rewiring already supplies Section 4s clearest worked example. Curvature-Gated Propagation  (Table 4)  lifts the discrete curvature κij introduced above for edge addition and removal (Topping et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023) and reuses it instead as gate inside the propagation filler Pk of an otherwise ordinary spatial layer, level 2 move because that gated operator is not yet in the catalogued inventory. Importing an already-cataloged rewired operator, say spectral-gap-increasing rewiring native to one family, as the {P(ℓ) } filler of different family is instead level 1. virtual node only fits this same recombination reading when the host layers domain and channel set can absorb the extra vertex without changing type. Treating it as first-class second domain still does not by itself produce level 3 expansion because the graded extension already admits multiple typed domains and inter-rank channels. The Sequential Co-Lifted NodeEdge Layer in Section 4.2 reaches Level 3 only because its added schedule makes the node update consume the newly written edge state within the same macro-layer. B.3 Skip and Residual Connections Residual connections let layers output retain copy of an earlier state. They are the standard remedy for the vanishing-signal and oversmoothing problems that limit depth (Section 5.1). Under the contraction conditions of Theorem 2 (notably µ < 1), repeated propagation without residual drives all node states toward the degree-dominated subspace. An initial residual can keep each node anchored away from that limit. The energy floor of Theorem 3 is proved for the initial-residual (PPR) iteration specifically, and generic residual need not by itself guarantee escape from the smoothing subspace. ℓ<ℓ S(ℓ) ℓ H(ℓ)W(ℓ) ℓ , where W(ℓ) Primary location. The ego/residual map Bℓ, which Section 3 routes into the update ϕℓ as the ego term it receives. In the common case Bℓ(H(ℓ)) = H(ℓ) (identity residual). cross-layer skip generalizes this to read earlier layers, Bℓ(H(0), . . . , H(ℓ)) = ℓ Rdℓ dB,ℓ maps the earlier width to the width dB,ℓ expected by the ego-input argument of ϕℓ (for common additive update, dB,ℓ = dℓ+1), and ℓ Rnℓnℓ is per-layer mixing coefficient selecting which earlier states are re-injected (a scalar s(ℓ) S(ℓ) ℓ in the common node-preserving case, where nℓ = nℓ). To preserve permutation equivariance, S(ℓ) ℓ must itself be equivariant (in practice scalar multiple of the identity, or declared coarsening/alignment map when the node set changes), since an arbitrary fixed matrix would encode node identities. Reading every earlier state exceeds the single-step signature Bℓ(H(ℓ), H(0)) that Section 3 declares. The identity and initial residual fit it directly, whereas full multi-layer skip either requires the extended ego signature Bℓ(H(0), . . . , H(ℓ)) or, for dense jumping-knowledge aggregation, is deferred to the readout ρ (below), where reading the whole stack is native. Representative forms. An initial residual re-injects fixed, width-aligned initial representation G(0) at every layer, Bℓ(H(ℓ), H(0)) = α G(0), as in APPNP and GCNII (Appendix D, the spectral and polynomial-filter family). The anchor is the transformed input, not the raw features. APPNP teleports to G(0) = fθ(X) (an MLP of the input, distinct from the frameworks H(0) = X, and written rather than the frameworks reserved final-representation Z), and GCNII likewise anchors to an initial hidden representation. Keeping every node tied to its own input contributes to GCNIIs ability to train deeply, alongside its identity mapping in the weight path. dense skip (jumping-knowledge style) makes Bℓ read all previous layers and is most naturally folded into the readout ρ when the combination is deferred to the end (Xu et al., 2018). Reversible 93 residuals constrain Bℓ and ϕℓ so the forward map is invertible, trading recomputation for memory and enabling very deep stacks (Li et al., 2021). Composition note. The initial residual and the dense skip both write Bℓ, so they do not compose independently the way different-component operations do. Stacking them requires an explicit combination rule in that component, for example Bℓ(H(0), . . . , H(ℓ)) = αG(0) + ℓ , rather than two edits that pass through each other untouched. This is the same-component interaction the factorization flags. Same slot means reconcile, not necessarily choose one. ℓ H(ℓ)W(ℓ) ℓ<ℓ S(ℓ) Link to generated architectures. Because Bℓ is one of the seven recombinable components, moving an existing residual scheme into family that does not natively use it is level 1: Table 4 marks Spectrally-Gated Propagation and Curvature-Gated Propagation with the same linear-specialization ego/update pair () precisely because both borrow the plain identity residual for Bℓ rather than proposing new one. genuinely new ego map, for instance combination rule for stacked initial and dense skips (the Composition note above) that is not already catalogued, would instead be level 2. B.4 Normalization Normalization rescales or recenters representations to stabilize training and, in the graph setting, to counter oversmoothing by preventing node states from collapsing together. Primary location. Most commonly the update map ϕℓ, but the placement depends on where the normalization map ν is inserted. Post-update normalization wraps the output, ϕℓ 7 ν ϕℓ, and leaves the operator bank and message map untouched. Pre-activation normalization sits inside the update, ϕℓ(a, b) = σ(ν(a + b)), still within ϕℓ. Pre-normalization of the state before propagation, = ν(H) with Pk = Pk( H) and Ψk = Ψk( H), as in pre-norm transformer blocks, instead feeds state-dependent operator and message, so it reaches Pk and Ψk rather than ϕℓ alone. Normalization is therefore clear case of the primary-component caveat. Its primary component is ϕℓ, but the pre-norm variant is not operator-preserving. PairNorm, GraphNorm, and graph-level batch/instance normalizations generally couple several node rows. When they are folded into ϕℓ, they therefore use the generalized permutation-equivariant update allowed by Theorem 1, not the stricter node-local row-wise specialization used by some results in Appendix C. Those row-wise results do not automatically extend to cross-node normalization unless the normalizations equivariance and the particular proof assumptions are checked separately. Representative forms. Generic batch and layer normalization carry over from deep learning unchanged. Graph-specific variants exploit graph structure. PairNorm centers and rescales node representations so their aggregate pairwise distance is fixed to prescribed scale, opposing the contraction that causes oversmoothing rather than conserving the incoming distance across the layer (Zhao & Akoglu, 2020). GraphNorm normalizes each graph separately and learns feature-wise mean-shift parameter, acting as trainable preconditioner that retains useful graph-level information (Cai et al., 2021). DropEdge is closely related regularizer. It randomly removes edges during training, stochastic perturbation of the operator bank rather than normalization in any exact sense (Rong et al., 2020). It only loosely rescales propagation intensity: because the degree-normalization map η is nonlinear, the expected normalized operator of the dropped graph need not be rescaling of the clean one. E[η(Adrop)] need not equal η(A) for any constant (such as the edge keep-probability), though special graphs or distributions may coincide, so the normalization reading is heuristic, not an identity in expectation. Link to generated architectures. Reusing an existing graph-specific normalization as the ϕℓ filler, or for pre-normalization the Pk/Ψk filler, of family that does not natively normalize that way is again level 1 recombination. normalization rule outside the current inventory would instead be level 2 if folded into ϕℓ under the generalized permutation-equivariant update Theorem 1 allows, since PairNorm and GraphNorm already show that cross-node normalization can satisfy that broader hypothesis without being row-wise. 94 B.5 Pooling and Readout Graph-level tasks require single vector per graph. Pooling produces it, either in one shot (global readout) or hierarchically (coarsening the graph in stages). Primary location. For flat, global pooling, this is the post-stack readout ρ alone, permutation-invariant aggregate over the final node states (Section 2.8). For hierarchical pooling, the affected core components are the per-layer domain and operator bank {P(ℓ) }. They are edited between layers through the auxiliary coarsening map Qℓ below. This map is outside the seven-component per-layer tuple and is also distinct from the post-stack readout ρ; ρ still acts only once, at the end, on whatever domain the coarsening has produced by the final layer. Representative forms. Flat readouts sum, average, or max node states; the sum is the form that can be made injective on multisets. The raw sum is not itself injective (distinct multisets can share total), and an injective pointwise encoding does not by itself fix this (its summed values can still collide). For bounded-size multisets over countable state space, however, there is specially chosen encoding for which 7 xS (x) is injective, and an injective post-map then preserves the distinction. This is the property GIN (Xu et al., 2019b) relies on for expressiveness. Learned hierarchical poolings include differentiable soft cluster assignment, which learns soft map of nodes to smaller node set (Ying et al., 2018b); score-based node selection, which keeps top-k subset by learned score (Lee et al., 2019; Gao & Ji, 2019); and spectral methods that pool by relaxed min-cut objective (Bianchi et al., 2020). The choice interacts with the readout. Hierarchical pooling changes the domain on which ρ ultimately acts. Formal mechanics. Hierarchical pooling is written in the unified equation as node-to-cluster map H(ℓ+1) (Section 3.2). For Qℓ Rnℓ+1nℓ applied to the node-preserving intermediate state, H(ℓ+1) = Qℓ , followed by reconstruction of {P(ℓ+1) assignment-based pooling common choice is A(ℓ+1) = QℓA(ℓ)Q }; ℓ selection-based and topology-aware poolings instead define the next graph directly. For the layer to stay equivariant, Qℓ must itself be computed equivariantly. Under source-node relabeling Π and the induced target-cluster relabeling Πout, Qℓ(ΠAΠ, ΠH) = Πout Qℓ(A, H) Π; fixed arbitrary Qℓ would instead encode node identities and break the symmetry. When an initial residual continues across pooling, the teleport target is realigned to the current domain by the composition of the coarsening maps applied so far. This composition is Qℓ1 Q0H(0), where each Qt maps layer ts output domain to layer t+1s. This realignment carries feature projection when d0 = dℓ+1. Link to generated architectures. Flat pooling acts only through the external readout ρ, which none of the three generation levels of Section 4 constrain, so choosing or designing ρ is orthogonal to architecture generation. It can be paired with Level 1, Level 2, or Level 3 layer without itself counting as slot-filling move. Hierarchical pooling is the partial exception. Because it edits and {P(ℓ) } between layers through Qℓ, adopting an existing coarsening scheme in family that does not natively pool is the same level 1 recombination as for any other per-layer component, while genuinely new equivariant Qℓ would be level 2. B.6 Continuous-Depth and ODE Views residual layer H(ℓ+1) = H(ℓ) + (H(ℓ)) is one explicit Euler step of size of the ODE H(t) = (H(t)) (the standard residual is the unit step = 1). The continuous-depth view takes this seriously. Depth becomes integration time, and the layer update is read as discretized dynamical system rather than fixed stack. In the narrow case, pure discrete-to-continuous reinterpretation, this is the update Primary location. ϕℓ. The same propagation operators {P(ℓ) } supply the right-hand-side dynamics, and only the integrator that assembles them into depth-varying map changes. This is why we class it as an operation rather than family. Broader ODE architectures go further than the integrator and edit other slots too. second-order or otherwise augmented dynamics enlarges the per-object state (a velocity channel appended to H, on the same node domain , not new set of graph objects). Such dynamics can also change the message Ψk, the update ϕℓ, or the operator Pk, the components that define the vector field. The domain changes only 95 if new objects are introduced. The classification is clean only for the reinterpretation; the augmented case spans several components. Representative forms. sections.title: Appendix C Theoretical Analysis
sections.content: Overview. The four subsections that follow answer four different questions about the same object, the propagation bank {Pk} together with the slots that surround it. Section C.1 asks which named architectures are exact special cases of the unified equation, and shows that spectral filters, multi-hop models, and attention layers are recovered as particular fillings, differing only along small number of axes localized to specific slots. Sections C.2 and C.3 ask what the propagation bank can and cannot do. The first bounds reach (what node can see, and what it takes for one layer to mix everything), and the second bounds behavior under depth (when repeated propagation collapses information, and two component-level mechanisms analyzed here that can prevent it: the ego/residual map Bℓ and the propagation bank Pk). Section C.4 closes with two conditional structural boundaries: ceiling on what structure-blind components can distinguish, and the equivariance conditions the component maps and operators must satisfy to define permutation-consistent graph layer. Several results restate established facts, including oversmoothings geometric decay, polynomialfilter universality, and the 1-WL ceiling. Their role is to verify that the component vocabulary preserves known theory across architectural families. The results specific to the decomposition are the slot-level 97 attribution and identifiability consequences. They include the fact that channel count is not identifiable while channel rank is, that one-layer global mixing has precise necessary condition on the support of Pk, and that oversmoothing is escaped through more than one slot-level mechanism, chiefly the ego/residual map Bℓ and the spectral filling of Pk. Notation/Conventions. Each result names the slots and assumptions it constrains, so design choice can be traced to the relevant columns rather than only to named architecture. Table 12 groups results by the property they establish, following the four-part organization above. Because the grouping is thematic rather than sequential, the Theorem/Lemma/Proposition numbers do not always run consecutively within subsection below. Lemma 2, Proposition 4, and Theorem 1 are each numbered earlier than the results they are grouped with, since their thematic home is later subsection. The recast-standard results (contraction, the energy bound, realizability, universality, the WL ceiling, aggregation injectivity) show that the framework reproduces known facts in single notation; the additional slot-level consequences developed here include channel-rank identifiability (in the linear regime, where the layer depends on the channels only through = Pk), the full-row condition for one-layer globality under the propositions hypotheses, and the localization of two principal smoothing escapes in the ego/residual map Bℓ and the spectral filling of Pk.
